opus-5.5.text:
Well, I look at it first as a practical matter, and then as a question of fairness, because people tend to jump straight to the fairness part.

The reason it's coming up is that we have very large wealth gaps and very large government debts, and those two things together historically produce pressure to go after wealth. I've studied this over hundreds of years, and when you have big deficits, big gaps between the rich and the poor, and political conflict, you tend to get wealth taxes or something like them. So I understand why it's happening, and I do think those gaps are a real problem that has to be dealt with. If you don't deal with them, you get a kind of internal conflict that's bad for everybody, including the rich.

But as an investor and a mechanic of how the machine works, I'd say a wealth tax has serious problems. The first is that wealth is mobile. Taxing it can be like trying to catch something that moves. People and their capital can leave, and when they leave, you lose them, their productivity, and the income tax they were paying. The second is that most wealth isn't sitting in cash. It's in things like private companies and illiquid assets. They're difficult to value, and to pay the tax you may have to sell them, which takes capital away from productive uses. Third, the amount of money you'd raise is usually small relative to the size of the deficit, so it doesn't solve the problem it's supposed to solve.

So my view is that the wealth gap and the debt have to be addressed, but a wealth tax by itself is likely to be a poor way of doing it. What you really want is to grow the pie and divide it well: productivity, education, equal opportunity, and a tax system that works and that people see as fair. And it has to be done in a bipartisan, thoughtful way, because the alternative to reasoned compromise is conflict, and history shows us that's when things get really ugly.

r001.rationale: The response says illiquid assets may need to be sold to pay the tax.

r002.rationale: It mentions asset sales but does not say they can burst an asset bubble.

r003.rationale: It says paying the tax may take capital away from productive uses, communicating reduced investment.

r004.rationale: It recommends productivity and other measures as a better approach, but does not recommend pairing them with wealth taxation.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss transfer payments redirecting investment funds to consumption or their effect on productivity.

r006.rationale: It does not advocate a minimum standard of living for people who are not economically productive.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying I'm a practical person, not an ideological one. So when I look at a wealth tax, I don't ask whether it feels fair or unfair. I ask: does it work? What happens mechanically when you do it?

And the first thing you have to understand is that we have a wealth gap that is enormous. The top one tenth of one percent has roughly the same net worth as the bottom ninety percent. That's not sustainable in a democracy. When you have that kind of gap, combined with a big values gap, historically you get populism of the left and populism of the right, and then you get a fight. I've studied the last five hundred years of these cycles, and that's the pattern. So something has to be done. I'm not against redistribution. I think the system needs to be reformed so that it produces opportunity and productivity for most people, not just a few.

But the question is how. A wealth tax, as it's typically proposed, has a few problems that are mechanical, not political. Wealth is mostly not cash. It's ownership of businesses, of property, of things that are hard to value. So you have to value it every year, and you're going to fight over that valuation. Then the person has to raise cash to pay the tax, which often means selling assets, and when a lot of people sell assets at the same time, that affects markets and capital formation. And then the third thing, which is the big one, is that money and people move. If you tax wealth in one place and not another, capital leaves. We've seen that in Europe. Most of the countries that tried wealth taxes got rid of them, not because they didn't like the idea but because they didn't raise much money and they drove capital out. California or New York doing it alone is even worse than a country doing it, because moving to Florida or Texas is very easy.

So what I'd rather see is this. First, broaden the base and tax income and gains in a way that's harder to escape, including things like carried interest and the step-up in basis at death, which I think are hard to justify. Second, and this is the part people miss, the money has to be spent productively. If you just redistribute it into consumption, you've shrunk the pie and you're still unequal, just poorer. If you put it into education, into early childhood, into things that raise the productivity of people at the bottom, then you get a return on that money. It's an investment, not a cost. That's the bipartisan deal I'd like to see: the people with wealth give up more, but it goes into things that demonstrably produce productive citizens.

And I'd add one more thing. I'd rather be in a system where the wealthy do this voluntarily and in partnership with government than one where we get there through conflict. Because if we don't reform it, history says it gets reformed for us, and that's usually a lot uglier.

r001.rationale: It says wealth holders may have to raise cash to pay the tax, often by selling assets.

r002.rationale: It says asset sales can affect markets and capital formation, but does not say they can burst an asset bubble.

r003.rationale: It says wealth-tax-driven asset sales can affect capital formation, communicating reduced investment.

r004.rationale: It recommends directing tax revenue to education and early childhood programs that raise productivity.

r005.rationale: It says redistribution into consumption shrinks the pie, while investment in productivity-raising programs yields a return.

r006.rationale: It does not advocate maintaining a minimum standard of living for people who are not economically productive.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with what you’re trying to accomplish. If the objective is to create more opportunity and a society that works well for most people, I’m sympathetic to that. But then you have to ask: how would a wealth tax actually work?

Wealth isn’t necessarily cash sitting in a bank account. It might be ownership in a business. So how do you value it, how do you collect the tax, and what behavior does that create? Does it cause capital to move? Does it affect investment? Those consequences matter.

And then there’s the other side: what do you do with the money? If you invest it effectively in education and opportunities that enable people to become productive, that can benefit everybody. Collecting more money doesn’t, by itself, establish that you’ve solved the problem.

So I’d assess it as a whole system: fairness, incentives, practicality, and the effectiveness of the spending. The goal should be broader prosperity, and we should judge the policy by whether it actually produces that.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention asset sales bursting an asset bubble.

r003.rationale: It asks whether the tax would affect investment but does not state that wealth taxation will reduce investment.

r004.rationale: It recommends investing tax proceeds in education and opportunities that help people become productive.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss transfer payments or funds shifting from productive investment to consumption.

r006.rationale: The response does not advocate maintaining a minimum standard of living for people who are not economically productive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between the objective and the mechanism. The objective—having a society in which people have opportunity, in which we invest in education and basic needs—is very important. I believe those who have more should contribute more, including me.

Then the question is: how do you do that well? Wealth is not the same as cash. Somebody might own a business, and you have to decide how to value it and whether they have to sell part of it to pay the tax. You also have to consider how people will respond, including moving their capital.

So I wouldn’t assess it simply by whether it sounds fair. I’d ask: how much revenue does it actually produce, what are the consequences, and is that money being used productively? We need to address the opportunity gap. But we need a system that does that effectively while preserving the incentives to create and invest.

r001.rationale: It says a business owner may have to sell part of the business to pay the tax, identifying asset sales to obtain cash as a possible requirement.

r002.rationale: It does not say that wealth-tax-driven asset sales can burst an asset bubble.

r003.rationale: It raises possible responses such as moving capital and says incentives should be preserved, but does not state that taxing wealth will reduce investment.

r004.rationale: It calls for using revenue productively and preserving incentives, but does not recommend pairing wealth taxes with measures that improve productivity.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss transfer payments shifting funds from productive investment to consumption or their effect on societal productivity.

r006.rationale: It supports investing in basic needs and addressing the opportunity gap, but does not advocate a minimum standard of living specifically for people who are not economically productive.
